runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I

This chapter has almost no new teaching. It lists what you should be comfortable with from Chapters 1 to 16, and it sends you back to those chapters for extra study. Use it as a checklist before the five review labs.
1.1 Chapter 1: Getting Started with Red Hat Enterprise Linux
You should be able to explain what open source, Linux, a Linux distribution and Red Hat Enterprise Linux are.
Think of a recipe that anyone may read, change and share: that is
packs the kernel with tools into a complete system, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux is Red Hat's supported one.
Linux is the core; a distribution is the full package; RHEL is Red Hat's.
You should be able to log in on a text console or the GNOME desktop and run simple commands in the shell.
is the program that reads your typed commands, like a waiter taking orders;
is the shell used in this course. Tab completion finishes names, command history brings back old commands, and editing shortcuts fix a line without retyping it.
Tab, history and editing shortcuts save typing.
1.3 Chapter 3: Managing Files From the Command Line
You should be able to move around the file system and copy, move, create, delete and link files.
Files sit in a tree of directories, like folders in a filing cabinet. A

path starts where you are now.

Know absolute and relative paths, links, and pattern matching.
1.4 Chapter 4: Getting Help in Red Hat Enterprise Linux
You should be able to find answers on the system itself, in manual pages and GNU Info.
Think of an instruction manual built into the machine.
Look in the manual pages and GNU Info first.
1.5 Chapter 5: Creating, Viewing, and Editing Text Files
You should be able to redirect output, use pipes, edit with vim, and use shell variables.

1.6 Chapter 6: Managing Local Users and Groups
You should be able to manage accounts, groups, administrator access and password policy.
Accounts are like key cards: each
lends the master key for one command. You can create, change and delete users and groups, set a password policy, and lock or unlock accounts.
You should be able to read and change file permissions and ownership.
are read, write and execute rights for the owner, the group and everyone else, like house keys for family, friends and strangers. Command-line tools such as
sets the default permissions of new files, and special permissions can make new files in a directory belong to that directory's group.
Owner, group, others; and the umask sets the defaults.
1.8 Chapter 8: Monitoring and Managing Linux Processes
You should be able to see what runs on a system and control it.
is a running program, like a worker on a shop floor. You should be able to check each one's status, resource use and owner, manage several tasks from one terminal with Bash
, and end processes or user sessions.
tells you how busy the system is.
Find the busy process, then control or end it.
You should be able to list and control services with systemd and
is a background program that waits for work, like a receptionist.
is the manager that starts and stops them, and
is the tool you use to control them.
controls the daemons that systemd manages.
You should be able to log in with
, set up key-based login, and restrict root and password logins.
is an encrypted remote login. A
is like a lock and its unique key: the lock goes on the server and the key stays with you, so no password travels. You can also forbid direct root login and password logins in the OpenSSH service.
Keys instead of passwords, and no direct root login.
You should be able to read logs and the journal, keep the journal across reboots, and keep time correct.
Logs are the system's diary. The
is the systemd log, and syslog files record events too.
(Network Time Protocol) keeps the clock right, and the time zone makes time stamps readable.
Read the diary, keep it across reboots, and keep the clock right.

You should be able to identify storage devices, mount file systems, and search for files.
is storage that is read and written in fixed-size blocks, such as a disk.
attaches a file system to a directory, like plugging a drawer into a cabinet.
Identify the device, mount it on a directory, then find files.
1.16 Chapter 16: Analyzing Servers and Getting Support
You should be able to use the Web Console, the Red Hat Customer Portal and Red Hat Insights.
is a browser dashboard for managing and watching a server. The
is a help center with documentation and the Knowledgebase.
analyzes servers for problems, helps fix them, and confirms the fix.
Dashboard, help center, and problem finder.
the earlier chapters of the book, and the Study file for each chapter.
A small team needs a new server,
. Everything you reviewed has a part in the job.
Set up: log in with SSH keys (Chapter 10), create the team's users and groups (Chapter 6), set the network and host name (Chapter 12), and install software (Chapter 14).
Run: start and enable services (Chapter 9), set file permissions (Chapter 7), and mount the storage the team will use (Chapter 15).
Look after: read the logs (Chapter 11), back up with
(Chapter 13), and ask Red Hat for help when you are stuck (Chapter 16).
Big picture: Set up, then Run, then Look after.
